newsitem.title: USA: CIA chief booed while discussing drugs in L.A.
newsitem.headline: CIA chief booed while discussing drugs in L.A.

text.p: In an unprecedented visit to a poor, drug-infested Los Angeles neighborhood, CIA Director John Deutch on Friday told angry residents there was no evidence the intelligence agency was involved in drug trafficking.
"Our purpose is to stop drugs from coming into the United States," Deutch told a skeptical audience that booed him as he was introduced.

The "town hall"-type meeting followed a series of articles in the San Jose Mercury News in August suggesting the Central Intelligence Agency had been involved in financing the Contra rebels fighting Nicaragua's Sandinista government in the 1980s through the smuggling of crack cocaine into poor sections of Los Angeles.
Deutch did not specifically deny the allegations, but told residents of South-Central Los Angeles that he was awaiting the outcome of an internal CIA investigation.
"As of today, we have no evidence of a conspiracy by the CIA to engage in drug trafficking," he said.
Deutch told the hostile audience that CIA employees "understand the harm (of drugs)" and shared their concerns.

The meeting in a high-school gymnasium, called by community activists, was attended by about 400 mostly black residents who were openly hostile towards Deutch. The room was ringed by CIA security men and there was a heavy contingent of police around the school.
It was clear from opening remarks by U.S. Rep. Juanita Millender-McDonald, that the neighborhood was rife with skepticism towards CIA statements that it had not sold crack on the streets.
"It is not up to us to prove the CIA was involved in drug-trafficking in South-Central L.A.; rather it is up to them to prove that they were not," she said.
"We are sick and tired of your excuses," one activist said when he came to the microphone in a question-and-answer session after Deutch's address.

The room exploded in applause when one woman blamed the situation on ex-President Ronald Reagan's firing of striking air traffic controllers, resulting in laxer controls of flights into the United States.
A stream of residents came to the microphone to condemn the scourge of drugs and describe different conspiracy theories.
After 90 minutes, Deutch stood up to say: "I go away with a better appreciation of what's on your mind."
